Tier 2 — Trade-off

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The three properties, as the spec states them — RFC 8446 §1: Introduction

  • Practical overview — MDN: Transport Layer Security

  • Where identity is actually established — RFC 8446 §4.4.2: Certificate

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three properties? Confidentiality, integrity, authentication (identity).
Which one actually fails in practice? Identity — expired, misissued, or unverified certificates. Never the cipher.
What does TLS not give you? Authorization, availability, or any guarantee the peer is well-behaved.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

TLS gives you three things and people rank them backwards. Confidentiality — nobody on the path reads your traffic — is what everyone names, and it's the part that essentially never fails. Integrity — nobody modifies it undetected — is invisible until it's missing, and it's what stops an injection attack from a coffee-shop router. Identity — you're talking to who you think — is the hard one, the one that requires a whole PKI to make work, and the one that actually breaks in production. Every real TLS outage I've seen was an identity problem: an expired certificate, or a verification someone turned off.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why is identity the hard property when encryption gets all the attention?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand that encryption without authentication is worthless, and can say why.

Because encryption alone is trivially defeatable. If you establish an encrypted channel without verifying who's on the other end, an attacker in the path simply terminates your connection, presents their own key, and opens a second encrypted connection onward — a machine-in-the-middle. You get a beautiful padlock and an encrypted conversation with the attacker. Confidentiality is preserved in the technical sense and completely useless in the practical one. So identity isn't one of three co-equal properties; it's the one the other two depend on for their meaning.

Making identity work is also disproportionately hard. Confidentiality and integrity are solved by mathematics that has been stable for years — pick an AEAD cipher and you're done. Identity requires an answer to "who vouches for this key?", which means certificate authorities, chains of trust, revocation, expiry, and a global agreement about which roots to trust. That's a sprawling operational system with dozens of failure modes, which is exactly why it's the part that breaks. The cipher suite has never taken down your service; a certificate that expired at 3am has.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Someone says "we don't need TLS internally, it's a private network". What's your answer?

📍 Seen in the wild: the perimeter-security argument, still common and worth being able to dismantle without being tedious about it.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can argue for internal TLS on grounds other than eavesdropping, which is the weakest of the three.

The eavesdropping argument is the weak one, so don't lead with it — inside a VPC, passive interception genuinely is harder. Lead with identity, because that's what a private network doesn't give you. Without TLS, your service identifies its callers by source IP, which means anything that can reach the address can impersonate anything else that can reach the address. A compromised pod, a misconfigured security group, a service that got rescheduled onto a shared subnet — all of them become authorized callers. "Private network" is a statement about routing, not about authentication, and treating a routing property as an identity property is precisely the assumption that lets one compromised workload move laterally through everything.

The second argument is integrity, which people forget entirely: without it, anything on the path can modify requests in flight, and a private network has plenty of things on the path — proxies, mesh sidecars, NAT devices, a compromised node. The third is that the cost has collapsed. Internal TLS used to mean managing certificates by hand, which is why the trade-off was real; a service mesh now issues and rotates them automatically, and symmetric encryption on modern hardware is a rounding error. So the honest framing is: the eavesdropping benefit is modest inside a VPC, the authentication benefit is large and unobtainable any other way, and the cost that made this a real debate has largely gone. That's a more persuasive argument than repeating "defence in depth".

4. Quick Comparison Table

Property What it stops Mechanism How it fails in practice
Confidentiality Reading your traffic AEAD symmetric encryption after key agreement Essentially never. Not your problem
Integrity Modifying traffic undetected The AEAD's authentication tag Never, in TLS 1.3 — the modes that could fail were removed
Identity (authentication) Talking to the wrong party Certificate chain validated to a trusted root Constantly: expiry, misissuance, verification disabled, wrong hostname
Not provided: authorization — — Your application's job. A valid cert says who, never what they may do
Not provided: availability — — TLS adds failure modes rather than removing them

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The dotted arrows are the point of the diagram. Confidentiality and integrity fall out of the key agreement almost for free — one ECDHE exchange gives you both, and TLS 1.3 permits only AEAD ciphers, which provide them in a single operation so the older "encrypt-then-MAC versus MAC-then-encrypt" configuration errors simply cannot occur. Identity is a separate, much larger machine, and it's what makes the other two mean anything.

Three checks must all pass for identity, and each is a distinct failure mode:

1. Chain validation — does the presented certificate chain to a root this client trusts? Fails on a missing intermediate, or a root the client doesn't have. 2. Hostname matching — does the certificate's SAN cover the name I asked for? Fails on a certificate that's valid but for the wrong name. 3. Validity window — is now between notBefore and notAfter? Fails on expiry, which is the single most common TLS outage in production.

And the fourth possibility, which isn't a check failing but a check not happening: verification disabled. curl -k, proxy_ssl_verify off, InsecureSkipVerify: true, a client library configured to accept any certificate. This is the most dangerous state because everything works perfectly — encrypted, integrity-protected, and authenticating nobody. Confidentiality without authentication is a private conversation with a stranger.

What TLS explicitly does not provide is worth stating because it's a common conflation: a valid certificate tells you who the peer is, never what they're allowed to do. Authorization is your application's problem, and mTLS in a mesh gives you a strong identity to authorize against, not the authorization itself.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't treat TLS as authorization. A valid client certificate proves identity and nothing else. Systems that grant access purely on "presented a cert from our CA" give every holder of any certificate from that CA full access — which in a mesh is every workload you run.

  • Don't disable certificate verification to fix a connection problem. InsecureSkipVerify and proxy_ssl_verify off are the standard way a temporary unblock becomes a permanent, silent hole: everything works afterwards, nothing errors, and no alert exists for it. If you must, put an expiry date and a ticket on it the same hour.

  • Don't rely on TLS for at-rest or in-process protection. It protects bytes on a wire between two endpoints. It says nothing about the data once terminated, logged, cached, or written to disk — and a terminating proxy holds plaintext in memory by design.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "HTTPS means the site is safe."

✅ Reality: It means the connection is confidential, unmodified, and to the name in the address bar. A phishing site with a valid certificate satisfies all three — it genuinely is paypa1-secure.com and your connection to it genuinely is private. TLS authenticates the name; it makes no claim about the operator's intentions.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I ranked these as encryption first, with identity as a supporting detail. It's the reverse: encryption without authentication is defeated by a machine-in-the-middle in one step, so identity is the property the other two depend on for meaning. That inversion also explains the operational picture — I have never had a cipher fail, and I have had certificates expire, and those two facts are the same fact.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • ../01-mental-models/01-osi-model.md — where TLS sits, and why it protects a session rather than a network

  • ../03-tcp-udp/19-tcp-vs-udp.md — the transport TLS assumes; DTLS is the UDP equivalent

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 37-tls13-handshake.md — how these three properties are actually established, and what each round trip buys

  • 38-certificates-chains-of-trust.md — the machinery behind identity, and where it breaks

  • 41-mtls.md — identity applied in both directions, which is what zero-trust rests on

📚 Reference Links

  • Protocol overview and handshake flow — RFC 8446 §2: Protocol Overview

  • 0-RTT data — RFC 8446 §2.3: 0-RTT Data

  • Resumption and pre-shared keys — RFC 8446 §2.2

  • 0-RTT replay, and why it's a design constraint — RFC 8446 §8: 0-RTT and Anti-Replay

  • Bonus — the practical overview: MDN: Transport Layer Security

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
RTT cost: 1.3 vs 1.2 vs 1.3 resumed? 1 RTT, 2 RTT, 0 RTT. On top of TCP's 1 RTT in every case.
How does 1.3 save a round trip? The client guesses the group and sends a key_share in the ClientHello.
What happens if the guess is wrong? HelloRetryRequest — you pay the extra RTT back, landing at 1.2's cost.
Why is 0-RTT dangerous? No replay protection: no round trip has happened, so no freshness is proven.
Is the certificate encrypted in 1.3? Yes. SNI is still in the clear — that's what ECH is for.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

TLS 1.3 completes in one round trip because the client gambles: it guesses which key-exchange group the server will pick and sends its key_share in the ClientHello, so the server can derive keys and send its certificate in the very first reply. TLS 1.2 needed two round trips because negotiation and key exchange were separate phases. On resumption, 1.3 offers 0-RTT — application data in the first flight — but that data has no replay protection, so it's safe only for idempotent requests. The gamble is why 1.3 is fast, and HelloRetryRequest is what it costs when it's wrong.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through how 1.3 gets to one round trip when 1.2 needed two.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the mechanism is speculative key exchange, or just that "1.3 is faster".

TLS 1.2 was strictly sequential. The ClientHello offered cipher suites; the server replied picking one and sending its certificate and key-exchange parameters; the client then sent its key-exchange message and finished. Two round trips, because the client could not begin key exchange until it knew which algorithm had been chosen — negotiation had to complete before key agreement could start.

TLS 1.3 collapses this by having the client guess. The ClientHello carries not just supported groups but an actual key_share — an ephemeral public key for the group the client thinks the server will choose, usually X25519. If the guess is right, the server has everything it needs immediately: it derives the shared secret, and its single reply carries ServerHello, its own key share, the encrypted extensions, the certificate and its Finished. The client sends Finished and application data. One round trip, and note the second consequence — because keys exist after the server's first message, everything from EncryptedExtensions onward is encrypted, including the certificate, which was sent in the clear in 1.2.

The gamble has a cost. If the client offers a group the server won't use, the server sends HelloRetryRequest naming an acceptable group, and the client retries with a correct key_share — costing exactly the round trip that was saved and landing you back at 1.2's latency. In practice this is rare because clients offer the group everyone supports, but it's the honest answer to "is 1.3 always 1-RTT?", and knowing it exists is a reliable depth marker.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Your CDN offers 0-RTT. Do you enable it, and for what?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard probe on this topic, because the wrong answer — treating 0-RTT as a free speed setting — is very common.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know 0-RTT trades a security property for latency, and can name which requests may make that trade.

Enable it, but only for safe methods. 0-RTT lets a returning client send application data in its very first flight using keys derived from a previous session, which removes the entire handshake from the critical path — on a 200ms path that's 200ms off time-to-first-byte for every returning visitor. The cost is that this data has no replay protection, and the reason is structural rather than an implementation gap: no round trip has occurred yet, so the server has received nothing proving this flight is fresh. An attacker who captures the first flight can resend it later and the server cannot distinguish the copy from the original.

So the rule is that 0-RTT data must be idempotent and non-state-changing. GET /article/123 is fine — a replay wastes a little work and reveals nothing new. POST /transfer is not, and neither is anything consuming a one-time token or incrementing a counter. In practice you configure the edge to accept early data only for safe methods and defer everything else to the full 1-RTT handshake, which is what mainstream CDNs do by default. RFC 8446 §8 also describes anti-replay mechanisms — single-use tickets and a bounded replay window — which reduce the exposure without eliminating it, so they're defence in depth rather than a reason to relax the rule. There's a second, quieter caveat worth naming: early data has weaker forward-secrecy properties than the rest of the connection, which is another reason to keep genuinely sensitive payloads off it. The design answer is that 0-RTT is a per-request decision, not a per-connection switch.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

You terminate TLS for 200,000 new connections a second at the edge. What runs out?

📍 Seen in the wild: the capacity question behind every "why is TLS termination a separate tier?" discussion.

CPU, spent almost entirely on asymmetric crypto during the handshake. The steady-state cost of an established connection is symmetric encryption — AES-GCM with hardware acceleration, effectively free at a few cycles per byte. The handshake is different: the server does an ECDHE key agreement and, more expensively, an RSA or ECDSA signature over the transcript, and those are orders of magnitude costlier per operation. This is why TLS capacity is measured in handshakes per second, not gigabits, and why an edge fleet is sized by connection rate rather than throughput. The choice of key type matters here in a way people underestimate: ECDSA P-256 signing is several times cheaper than RSA-2048 signing, so serving an ECDSA certificate (with an RSA one alongside for legacy clients) is one of the largest single levers available.

It presents as CPU saturation that tracks new-connection rate while bytes-per-second stays flat — which defeats a capacity model keyed to bandwidth. The secondary limit is session-cache memory and coordination: resumption only helps if the ticket a client presents can be validated by whichever server it lands on, so a fleet without shared ticket keys silently degrades every resumption into a full handshake, and your resumption rate quietly falls without any error. Monitor handshakes per second, the full-versus-resumed ratio, and CPU per handshake segmented by key type. The architectural levers, in order: session resumption (turns most handshakes into cheap ones), connection reuse and keep-alive (removes handshakes entirely), ECDSA certificates, and only then more CPU.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design TLS for a global API where time-to-first-byte is the product metric.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat handshake cost as a placement problem before a protocol one.

The highest-stakes constraint is that handshake cost is round trips multiplied by distance, and nothing in the protocol changes the speed of light. A client in Mumbai reaching a us-east-1 origin pays roughly 200ms RTT, so TCP plus TLS 1.3 is ~400ms before the request is read — and TLS is only half of that. So the first decision isn't a TLS setting at all: terminate at an anycast edge PoP near the user, where the same two round trips cost ~40ms, and keep a warm pooled connection from edge to origin so the expensive long leg is paid once at pool-warm time rather than per request.

With placement settled, the protocol decisions stack on top. TLS 1.3 only — there is no remaining reason to offer 1.2 to a modern client population, and dropping it removes a round trip and a large amount of legacy cipher surface. Session resumption with fleet-wide shared ticket keys, rotated frequently, so a returning client lands at 0 or 1 RTT regardless of which edge server answers; without shared keys this silently fails and you'll never see an error. 0-RTT for safe methods only, per the Tier 2 rule, configured at the edge so the application never has to reason about it. And HTTP/3 where available, because QUIC fuses transport and crypto into a single 1-RTT exchange and resumes at 0-RTT — the same idea applied one layer down, with an HTTP/2-over-TCP fallback since UDP is blocked often enough to matter.

The failure I'd monitor first is the resumption rate, not latency. It's the metric that silently collapses — a ticket-key rotation bug, a fleet scale-out that misses the shared key distribution, a client library that stops caching sessions — and when it does, every connection becomes a full handshake. Edge CPU rises, p99 rises, and nothing errors. Alert on the resumed-handshake fraction dropping below its baseline, and on certificate expiry dates well before they matter, because the other way TLS takes you down has nothing to do with performance.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Setup path RTTs before first app byte Certificate visible? When you get it
TCP + TLS 1.2, full 1 + 2 = 3 Yes, sent in clear Legacy clients — the concrete reason to drop 1.2
TCP + TLS 1.3, full 1 + 1 = 2 No, encrypted The modern default for a new connection
TCP + TLS 1.3, HelloRetryRequest 1 + 2 = 3 No Client guessed the wrong group; back to 1.2's cost
TCP + TLS 1.3, resumed (PSK) 1 + 1 = 2 Not sent Returning client with a valid ticket
TCP + TLS 1.3, 0-RTT 1 + 0 = 1 Not sent Resumption + idempotent request; accepts replay risk
QUIC, new connection 1 total No Transport and crypto fused
QUIC, 0-RTT resumption 0 Not sent The current floor
Reused connection 0 — The point of every pooling strategy

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Bring the key to the first meeting and guess which lock.

📖 Story

Under the old rules you met once to agree which lock would be used, then met again to exchange keys, then finally talked. Now you turn up to the first meeting already holding a key for the lock you expect — and if you guessed right, the other side opens the door and starts talking in the same breath. Guess wrong and they hand you back a note naming the correct lock, and you make the second trip you were trying to avoid.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • Meeting to agree the lock, then meeting to exchange keys = TLS 1.2's two sequential round trips

  • Turning up already holding a key = the key_share for a guessed group, sent in the ClientHello

  • Opening the door and talking in the same breath = ServerHello, certificate and Finished in one flight, already encrypted

  • The note naming the correct lock = HelloRetryRequest, which costs back the round trip you saved

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Three things follow from the shape of the 1.3 flight, and each is a discussion-weight detail.

The key_share is speculative. The client picks a group before knowing the server's preference. That single change is what removes the round trip, and HelloRetryRequest is the recovery path when the guess fails — the server names an acceptable group and the client retries, paying back exactly one RTT. Everything else about 1.3's speed follows from this one restructuring.

Encryption starts a message earlier than you'd expect. Once the server has the client's key share it can derive handshake keys immediately, so EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished are all protected. In TLS 1.2 the certificate travelled in plaintext, which meant a passive observer learned exactly which site you were visiting. In 1.3 they don't — except that SNI is still in the ClientHello in the clear, because the server needs it to choose a certificate before any keys exist. That's the remaining leak, and Encrypted Client Hello is the in-progress fix.

Forward secrecy is mandatory, not optional. TLS 1.3 removed RSA key transport and static Diffie-Hellman entirely, so every key exchange is ephemeral (EC)DHE. A server's long-term private key can no longer decrypt recorded past sessions, because it was never used to encrypt them — it only signs. This is the largest security change in 1.3 and it came with a real operational consequence: passive-decryption middleboxes that relied on RSA key transport stopped working, which is why some enterprises resisted the upgrade.

Round-trip arithmetic on a 200ms path, cold connection: TLS 1.2: TCP 1 + TLS 2 = 3 RTT = 600ms before the request is read. TLS 1.3: TCP 1 + TLS 1 = 2 RTT = 400ms. TLS 1.3 + 0-RTT: TCP 1 + TLS 0 = 1 RTT = 200ms. QUIC + 0-RTT: 0 RTT — request data rides the first packet. Each step removes one round trip, and on a long path a round trip is the largest single unit of latency in the system.

The cipher-suite change is worth one beat because it confuses people reading old material. A TLS 1.2 suite named everything: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 specifies key exchange, authentication, bulk cipher and MAC. A TLS 1.3 suite names only the AEAD and hash: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. Key exchange and authentication are negotiated through separate extensions, which is why the 1.3 suite list is five entries rather than hundreds — a deliberate reduction of the misconfiguration surface.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is time_appconnect minus time_connect in your client's breakdown — the TLS handshake in isolation — and the derived metric that actually drives capacity is handshakes per second, split full versus resumed. On a cross-region path the TLS round trip is a straight 15–30% of a small request's total latency, and every architectural pattern around it (edge termination, session resumption, connection pooling, HTTP/3) exists to amortise or delete it.

The second reason it matters is cost shape. TLS's expense is concentrated in the handshake's asymmetric crypto, so a fleet holding a million idle connections is comfortable while the same fleet churning 50,000 handshakes per second is CPU-bound. If your capacity model is keyed to bandwidth or request rate rather than connection rate, a client-side change that reduces connection reuse will saturate your edge without any of your dashboards predicting it.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# 1. Isolate the TLS handshake cost. appconnect - connect = TLS alone.
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'tcp:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer}\n' \
     https://example.com/

# 2. What was actually negotiated? Version, suite, and whether the session resumed.
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E 'Protocol|Cipher|Session-ID|Verify return code'

# 3. Prove resumption works. -reconnect does 5 connections; look for "Reused".
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -reconnect \
  </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -cE 'Reused|New'

# 4. Force 1.2 to see the round trip you're paying for on legacy clients.
curl -s -o /dev/null --tlsv1.2 --tls-max 1.2 \
     -w 'tls1.2 appconnect:%{time_appconnect}\n' https://example.com/
curl -s -o /dev/null --tlsv1.3 \
     -w 'tls1.3 appconnect:%{time_appconnect}\n' https://example.com/

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

curl against example.com from ap-south-1, origin in us-east-1, ~195ms RTT, cold connection:

📥 t=0ms       DNS cached, connection starting
    │
    ▼
🔒 [1] TCP handshake                      time_connect     0.196s  (+1 RTT)
    │
    ▼
🔑 [2] ClientHello + key_share X25519      →                t=196ms
    │       client guesses the group; no wait for negotiation
    ▼
🏛️ [3] ServerHello + key_share,            ←                t=391ms
    │       then ENCRYPTED: EncryptedExtensions,
    │       Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished
    │       time_appconnect = 0.391s        (+1 RTT — TLS 1.3 done)
    ▼
✅ [4] Client Finished + GET /             →                t=391ms
    │       rides the same flight, no extra wait
    ▼
⚙️ [5] Response first byte                 time_starttransfer 0.586s (+1 RTT)
    │
    ▼
🎯 [6] Total                                                 0.589s

--- same host, forced to TLS 1.2 ---
🔒 [7]  TCP handshake                       time_connect     0.196s
🔑 [8]  ClientHello (no key share)          →                t=196ms
🏛️ [9]  ServerHello + Certificate IN CLEAR  ←                t=391ms
🔑 [10] ClientKeyExchange + Finished        →                t=391ms
🏛️ [11] Server Finished                     ←                t=586ms
        time_appconnect = 0.586s            (+2 RTT)
🎯 [12] Total                                                 0.784s

[1] 196ms is the path RTT and every number below is a multiple of it. Nothing about TLS changes this term — only placement does.

[2] The ClientHello carries an actual X25519 public key, not merely a list of supported groups. This is the whole 1-RTT mechanism in one line. Had the server demanded a different group, a HelloRetryRequest here would push time_appconnect to 0.586s — identical to the 1.2 path at [11].

[3] One flight carries the server's key share plus four encrypted messages. The certificate is inside the encrypted portion, so a passive observer on this path cannot read it — contrast [9], where the same certificate is in plaintext.

[4] The client's Finished and the HTTP request go together, so the handshake costs exactly one RTT measured from the client, not one and a half.

[5–6] TLS accounts for 195ms of a 589ms total — a third of it, on a request whose server work is ~3ms.

[7–12] The 1.2 path spends 390ms in TLS instead of 195ms. The 195ms difference is one round trip, and it's the concrete version of "TLS 1.3 is faster" — worth having as a number rather than a claim.

10. When TO Use This

  • TLS 1.3 as the only offered version, wherever your client population allows it. It removes a round trip, mandates forward secrecy, encrypts the certificate, and shrinks the cipher-suite surface from hundreds of combinations to five. Offering 1.2 alongside is a compatibility decision, not a security one — make it deliberately and with a client-population number behind it.

  • Session resumption, always, with fleet-wide shared ticket keys. It converts the expensive asymmetric handshake into a cheap symmetric one and is the single largest lever on edge CPU. The shared-key part is what makes it work behind a load balancer.

  • 0-RTT for safe, idempotent methods only. Real latency win for returning clients, gated on the replay rule. Configure it at the edge so application code never has to reason about it.

  • Terminate close to the user. The handshake cost is round trips times distance, so placement beats protocol tuning. An edge PoP converts a 400ms handshake into a 40ms one — a bigger win than anything else in this list.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't enable 0-RTT globally. Early data has no replay protection, so applying it to state-changing requests turns a performance feature into a correctness bug — and one that's very hard to detect, because a replayed request looks entirely legitimate in your logs. Gate it on method at the edge.

  • Don't run a TLS-terminating fleet without shared session ticket keys. Resumption silently degrades to full handshakes when a client lands on a server that can't decrypt its ticket. Nothing errors; edge CPU and p99 just get worse, and the cause is invisible unless you're tracking the resumed-handshake fraction.

  • Don't keep TLS 1.2 enabled by default "for compatibility". It costs an extra round trip, sends the certificate in the clear, and permits key-exchange modes without forward secrecy. Decide with data on your actual client population rather than by inertia, and if you must keep it, scope it to the endpoints that genuinely need it.

  • Don't tune ciphers before checking placement and reuse. The common instinct on a slow TLS path is to fiddle with cipher preferences; the actual wins are, in order, terminating closer, reusing connections, resuming sessions, and using ECDSA certificates. Cipher choice is a rounding error next to a saved round trip.

  • Don't assume 1.3 is always 1-RTT. HelloRetryRequest puts you back at two, and a client offering an unusual group population will trigger it. If your handshake timings are bimodal with a cluster at double the expected cost, this is the first thing to check.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "TLS 1.3 is faster because it uses faster cryptography."

✅ Reality: The bulk cipher work was already negligible — AES-GCM with hardware acceleration costs a few cycles per byte. The saving is one round trip, achieved by having the client send a speculative key_share in the ClientHello so negotiation and key exchange happen together. It's a protocol restructuring, not a cryptographic speedup.

❌ Misconception: "0-RTT is just resumption with the handshake skipped, so it's strictly better."

✅ Reality: It has no replay protection, and that's structural rather than an implementation gap — no round trip has happened, so nothing proves the flight is fresh. It's safe only for idempotent requests, and RFC 8446 §8's anti-replay measures reduce exposure without removing it.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I assumed TLS 1.3 encrypted everything from the ClientHello onward, so a passive observer learned nothing about where I was connecting. SNI is still in the clear — it has to be, because the server needs the hostname to pick a certificate before any keys exist. So the certificate is now hidden but the destination hostname isn't, which is exactly the gap Encrypted Client Hello exists to close. Realising that reframed 1.3's privacy improvement as partial rather than complete.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Saying "1.3 is one round trip" without the mechanism. Everyone knows the number. The load-bearing detail is why — the speculative key_share — and volunteering HelloRetryRequest as its failure mode is what separates recall from understanding.

Treating 0-RTT as a pure win. It's a trade of replay safety for a round trip, and it's a per-request decision. An answer that recommends it unconditionally invites exactly the follow-up you don't want.

Ignoring that TLS sits on top of TCP. The full cold-start cost is 2 RTT, not 1, and on QUIC it's 1 total rather than 2. Quoting the TLS number alone consistently understates what the user actually waits for.

Not knowing forward secrecy became mandatory. TLS 1.3 removed RSA key transport and static DH entirely. This is the biggest security change in the version and it has a real operational consequence — passive-decryption middleboxes stopped working — which is a good concrete detail to have ready.

Reaching for cipher tuning. On a slow HTTPS path the answer is almost never the cipher suite. It's placement, connection reuse, resumption, and key type. An answer that starts at cipher preferences signals unfamiliarity with where the time actually goes.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
TLS 1.3 full handshake 1 RTT On top of TCP's 1 RTT RFC 8446 §2
TLS 1.2 full handshake 2 RTT The round trip 1.3 removes RFC 8446 §2 (comparison)
TLS 1.3 resumption (PSK) 1 RTT, or 0 with early data Ticket issued via NewSessionTicket RFC 8446 §2.2, §2.3
0-RTT replay protection None inherent Anti-replay in §8 bounds but doesn't remove exposure RFC 8446 §8
HelloRetryRequest cost +1 RTT Wrong group guessed; lands back at 1.2's latency RFC 8446 §4.1.4
TLS 1.3 cipher suites 5 defined Names only AEAD + hash; 1.2 named everything RFC 8446 §B.4
Certificate visibility Encrypted in 1.3, plaintext in 1.2 SNI remains in the clear in both RFC 8446 §2
Forward secrecy Mandatory in 1.3 RSA key transport and static DH removed RFC 8446 §1.2

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency One RTT saved versus 1.2, one more removable via 0-RTT at the cost of replay safety; distance still dominates all of it
💰 Cost Handshake CPU is asymmetric crypto and scales with connection rate, not bytes — ECDSA over RSA is the cheapest large lever
🔒 Security Mandatory forward secrecy and an encrypted certificate, against 0-RTT's replay exposure and SNI still leaking the destination
📈 Scale Resumption is the scaling mechanism, and it depends on shared ticket keys across the fleet — a distributed-state problem hiding inside a crypto setting
🔧 Ops complexity Ticket-key rotation, certificate lifecycle and version policy are three separate ongoing obligations, each of which can cause an outage
🐛 Debuggability Encrypting the certificate improves privacy and removes a field packet captures used to rely on; openssl s_client remains the tool that answers most questions

16. Real World Usage

TLS 1.3's deployment was shaped by middleboxes, not by cryptography. Early drafts failed to connect through a meaningful fraction of enterprise networks because middleboxes inspected fields that had changed meaning. The fix was version negotiation via the supported_versions extension, with the legacy version field frozen at 1.2 so old middleboxes see something familiar — deliberate protocol camouflage, and the same ossification problem that later drove QUIC's decision to encrypt its transport header.

Enterprise passive decryption broke, and that was the point. Mandatory forward secrecy means a server's private key can no longer decrypt recorded traffic, which invalidated a common inspection architecture. The industry's answer was to move inspection to explicit terminating proxies rather than restore the weakness, and the resulting proposals for a "visibility" mode were rejected — a rare, clean case of the standards process refusing an operationally convenient security regression.

0-RTT is deployed widely and cautiously. Major CDNs enable early data by default only for safe methods, and this is worth citing as the pattern to copy: the platform enforces the idempotency rule so individual application teams don't have to get it right.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • TLS — Transport Layer Security. The successor name to SSL; every "SSL certificate" you'll ever be handed is a TLS certificate.

  • PSK — Pre-Shared Key. The mechanism behind 1.3 resumption: a ticket from an earlier session establishes a key both sides already hold, so the expensive asymmetric exchange can be skipped.

  • AEAD — Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data. A cipher mode providing confidentiality and integrity in one operation. TLS 1.3 permits only AEAD ciphers, which is why the older encrypt-then-MAC configuration errors are simply gone.

  • ECDHE — Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral. The key agreement in 1.3. "Ephemeral" is the load-bearing word: fresh keys per connection are what give forward secrecy.

  • ECH — Encrypted Client Hello. The in-progress mechanism to encrypt SNI, closing the last plaintext leak of the destination hostname.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 36-what-tls-gives-you.md — the three properties this handshake establishes, and the order people confuse them in

  • ../03-tcp-udp/20-three-way-handshake.md — the round trip TLS stacks on top of, and the arithmetic reused here

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 38-certificates-chains-of-trust.md — what the Certificate message contains and how it's validated

  • 40-termination-passthrough-reencryption.md — where in your topology this handshake happens, and what that costs

  • breadth.md (Cipher suites, forward secrecy & resumption) — the negotiation details this note summarises

  • ../06-http-versions/51-quic.md — the same handshake fused into the transport, saving another round trip

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • QUIC — transport and crypto in one 1-RTT exchange, 0-RTT on resumption; the current answer to setup cost

  • Connection pooling — not an alternative mechanism, the standard way to stop paying for this one

  • Edge termination — doesn't change the handshake, changes the distance it crosses, which matters more

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • ALPN — protocol selection rides inside this handshake at no extra round trip

  • SNI — how the server picks a certificate before keys exist, and the reason it must stay in the clear

  • Session resumption and ticket keys — the amortisation layer, and a distributed-state problem in its own right

19. System Design Application

Skipped — atomic mechanism; the architect-level treatment is discharged by the Section 3 Tier 4 follow-up (edge placement, resumption at fleet scale, and the metric to alert on). The system-level story for where TLS sits in a topology is owned by 40-termination-passthrough-reencryption.md.

Why do intermediates exist at all? Why not sign leaves directly from the root?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Why does certificate expiry cause total outages rather than degradation, and what do you do about it?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The Certificate message and chain ordering — RFC 8446 §4.4.2: Certificate

  • Certificate automation (ACME / Let's Encrypt) — RFC 8555: Automatic Certificate Management Environment

  • Practical overview — MDN: Transport Layer Security

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three tiers? Root (self-signed, in the trust store) → intermediate → leaf (your server).
What must the server send? Leaf and intermediates. Not the root — the client already has it.
Most common misconfiguration? Missing intermediate. Works in browsers with AIA fetching, fails in curl and Java.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Trust is delegated down a chain. A root CA is self-signed and lives in the client's trust store; it signs intermediates, which sign your leaf certificate. Validation walks upward: does the leaf's signature check against the intermediate, the intermediate's against the root, and is that root trusted? The server must send the leaf and the intermediates — not the root, which the client already has. Forget the intermediate and browsers often paper over it by fetching the missing cert, while curl, Java and Go fail hard. That asymmetry is why "it works in my browser" is the classic false negative here.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why do intermediates exist at all? Why not sign leaves directly from the root?

🎯 Really testing: whether you see the operational security reason, not just the structure.

Because the root's private key is the most valuable key in the system and must almost never be used. A root CA is in the trust stores of billions of devices, and those trust stores update slowly or never — so a compromised root cannot be revoked in any practical sense; you'd be waiting years for devices to age out. The defence is to keep the root offline, in hardware, powered on for a ceremony a handful of times in its life, and use it only to sign intermediates. Day-to-day issuance is done by intermediates that are online and therefore exposed.

That structure buys containment. If an intermediate is compromised, it can be revoked — clients check revocation for intermediates, and browsers ship blocklists — and the CA issues a new one without touching the root or any trust store. It also allows separation: different intermediates for different validation levels, regions, or customers, so a problem in one is scoped. The cost is the failure mode in the recall check: your server must present the intermediates, because the client has only the root, and a chain with a gap in it cannot be validated. That single operational requirement is behind most certificate misconfigurations in production.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Why does certificate expiry cause total outages rather than degradation, and what do you do about it?

📍 Seen in the wild: Microsoft Teams (Feb 2020), the Ericsson expiry that took down O2 and SoftBank mobile data (Dec 2018), and the Let's Encrypt DST Root CA X3 expiry (Sep 2021) that broke older Android and OpenSSL 1.0.2 clients.

🎯 Really testing: whether you alert on the right thing — the date, not the automation.

Because validity is a hard check with no grace period. At notAfter minus one second every connection succeeds; one second later every connection fails, for every client, simultaneously. There is no partial degradation to notice, no error rate creeping up, no canary. It's also the failure mode most likely to hit the whole service at once rather than a subset, because one certificate typically fronts everything. That combination — binary, total, time-triggered — is what makes it disproportionately represented in major outages relative to how simple the underlying problem is.

The mitigation people reach for is automation, and it's necessary but not sufficient. ACME (RFC 8555) with a 90-day certificate and renewal at 60 days is the standard, and it's genuinely good: short lifetimes force the automation to be exercised constantly, so it can't rot unnoticed the way an annual manual renewal does. But automation introduces its own silent failure — a renewal job erroring into a log nobody reads, a DNS-01 challenge failing after a nameserver change, a rate limit hit during a bulk re-issue. So the rule is: alert on days-until-expiry, not on renewal-job success. The expiry date is ground truth and remains true regardless of which part of your automation broke; job success only tells you about the failure modes you anticipated. Alert at 30, 14 and 7 days, on every certificate at every termination point, and monitor challenge success rates as a leading indicator. The other half is remembering that roots expire too — the DST Root CA X3 case broke clients whose trust stores had stopped updating, which no amount of diligence on your own certificate would have prevented.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Tier Signed by Where it lives Lifetime If compromised
Root Itself Client trust stores (OS, browser, JDK) 10–25 years Effectively unrevocable — the reason it stays offline
Intermediate Root Sent by your server, in the chain 5–10 years Revocable; new one issued without touching trust stores
Leaf Intermediate Your server 90 days typical (ACME), 398 max for public certs Revoke and reissue; short lifetime bounds the damage

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Validation walks upward from the leaf until it reaches something already trusted. Three things must hold at every step and one at the end: each signature verifies against the parent's public key, each certificate is within its validity window, none is revoked, and the topmost certificate reached is in the client's trust store. Separately, the leaf's Subject Alternative Name must cover the hostname requested — Common Name has been ignored for hostname matching by modern clients for years, so a certificate with the right CN and a missing SAN fails.

The operational asymmetry worth internalising:

The server sends: leaf + intermediates. The client already has the root and does not need it sent. Omit the intermediate and behaviour splits by client. Browsers frequently recover — they cache intermediates from previous sites and follow the AIA extension to fetch the missing one. curl, Java, Go, Python requests and most service-to-service clients do not, and fail with an unhelpful "unable to get local issuer certificate".

This is why "it works in my browser" is the classic false negative on this topic. Always test the chain with openssl s_client or an external checker, never with a browser.

Revocation deserves one honest beat because it mostly doesn't work. CRLs are large and stale; OCSP requires a live lookup that adds latency and leaks browsing to the CA, and clients historically soft-failed — treating an unreachable OCSP responder as "fine" — which makes it useless against an attacker who can block the lookup. OCSP stapling improves this by having the server fetch and attach a signed freshness proof, removing the client's lookup. But the real mitigation the industry converged on is short lifetimes: a 90-day certificate limits exposure by expiring rather than by being revoked, which is why ACME's short-lived default is a security design decision and not just an automation convenience.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't validate your chain with a browser. Browsers recover from missing intermediates via AIA fetching and cached intermediates, so a chain that's broken for every non-browser client can look perfect. Use openssl s_client -showcerts or an external chain checker.

  • Don't alert on renewal-job success instead of expiry date. A job that silently stopped running produces no failures to alert on. The date is ground truth; the job is one of several things that can break on the way there.

  • Don't rely on revocation to contain a compromise. OCSP soft-fail means a network-level attacker can suppress the check entirely, and CRLs are stale. Short lifetimes and fast reissue are the mechanism that actually works.

  • Don't assume only your certificate expires. Roots and intermediates expire too, and a root expiry breaks clients whose trust stores stopped updating — as the DST Root CA X3 expiry did to a large population of older Android devices in 2021. Nothing you do to your own leaf prevents it; knowing your client population's age does.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "The server sends the whole chain including the root."

✅ Reality: Leaf plus intermediates. Sending the root is harmless but pointless — the client either has it in its trust store or it doesn't, and a root it doesn't already trust isn't made trustworthy by being sent. What matters is that the intermediates are present, and that's the part most often missing.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated short certificate lifetimes as an automation convenience — a side effect of ACME making renewal cheap. It's a security design decision: revocation doesn't work reliably, so the industry replaced "revoke a bad certificate" with "every certificate expires soon anyway". Short lifetimes are the revocation mechanism, and once I saw that, 90-day certificates stopped feeling like a chore and started looking like the point.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 37-tls13-handshake.md — where the Certificate message sits in the flight, and that it's encrypted in 1.3

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 41-mtls.md — the same chain validation applied to the client, with an internal CA

  • 40-termination-passthrough-reencryption.md — each termination point is another certificate to manage and another expiry date

  • breadth.md (HSTS, pinning, rotation & ACME) — the automation and hardening layer around this

📚 Reference Links

  • What the handshake establishes, and where — RFC 8446 §2: Protocol Overview

  • SNI — the field that makes L4 routing possible without decrypting — RFC 6066 §3: Server Name Indication

  • Client certificates, and why they can only be checked at the terminator — RFC 8446 §4.4.2: Certificate

  • Bonus — the practical overview: MDN: Transport Layer Security

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three models, in one word each? Terminate (decrypt, stop), pass-through (never decrypt), re-encrypt (decrypt, re-encrypt).
What does pass-through cost you? Every L7 capability: path routing, WAF, header rewriting, per-request balancing and metrics.
What can an L4 device still route on? SNI — it's in the ClientHello in the clear. Hostname routing without decryption.
Where does client identity survive? Only at the terminator. Beyond it, you forward it in a header or lose it.
Cost of re-encryption? Two handshakes and two crypto operations per connection — roughly double the CPU.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three choices at every proxy hop. Terminate and the proxy decrypts, so it can route by path, run a WAF, rewrite headers and balance per request — but the traffic beyond it is plaintext. Pass through and the proxy forwards encrypted bytes it can't read, which preserves end-to-end encryption and costs you every L7 capability; you can still route by SNI, because that's in the clear. Re-encrypt and you decrypt, act, then open a fresh TLS connection to the backend — full visibility with encryption on both legs, at roughly double the crypto cost. The question is never which is best; it's what you're willing to be blind to.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

If a load balancer doesn't decrypt, what can it still do?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know SNI is plaintext, which is the whole reason L4 TLS routing exists at all.

Less than people expect, and more than they assume. It sees the TCP layer — source and destination addresses and ports, connection state, byte counts — so it can do connection-level load balancing, health checking at the TCP level, and rate limiting by source IP. What it cannot do is anything requiring the request: no routing by URL path, no Host-header rules, no header injection, no WAF inspection, no per-request balancing, no HTTP status codes in its metrics. A pass-through balancer's dashboard shows connections and bytes, not requests and 5xx rates, and that observability loss is usually the thing people regret rather than the routing limitation.

The one meaningful exception is SNI. The client's server name travels in the ClientHello in plaintext — it has to, since the server needs the hostname to choose a certificate before any keys exist. So an L4 proxy can peek at the first packet and route by hostname without terminating anything, which is how multi-tenant TCP front ends and TLS-passthrough ingress work. It's a genuinely useful middle ground: hostname-level routing with end-to-end encryption preserved. But it's hostname-level only — api.example.com versus app.example.com is decidable, /v1/users versus /v1/orders is not.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A regulated client says "no plaintext anywhere in your infrastructure". What do you build?

📍 Seen in the wild: the compliance framing that forces this decision to be explicit rather than inherited.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know re-encryption exists as a distinct third option, and can price it honestly.

Re-encryption, at every hop. The edge terminates the client's TLS — which you need, because without it there's no WAF, no path routing and no request-level observability — then opens its own TLS connection to the backend and forwards the request over that. Every wire is encrypted; no packet on any link carries plaintext. This is what an AWS ALB with an HTTPS target group does, what nginx does with proxy_pass https:// plus proxy_ssl_verify on, and what a service mesh does between sidecars. It's the default posture in regulated environments for exactly this reason.

The costs are real and worth naming before you're asked. Crypto roughly doubles: two handshakes and two encrypt/decrypt paths per request, which matters at the edge where handshake CPU is already the constraint — though backend connections are pooled and long-lived, so the second handshake amortises far better than the first. Certificate management doubles: your backends now need certificates too, plus a rotation story, which is why internal PKI or a mesh's automatic certificate issuance stops being optional. And the trust boundary needs actual thought — proxy_ssl_verify on with a pinned internal CA is meaningfully different from encrypting to a backend whose certificate you never check, and the second is common, gives you the encryption box ticked, and provides no authentication at all. The honest framing is that re-encryption buys you encryption-in-transit everywhere and does not by itself buy you mutual authentication; that's mTLS, and it's a separate decision.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

You terminate for 500 customer domains at one edge tier. What breaks first?

📍 Seen in the wild: the multi-tenant SaaS version, where certificate lifecycle rather than CPU is the thing that pages you.

Certificate lifecycle, and it fails discontinuously rather than degrading. CPU is a smooth curve you can watch and provision against; certificates work perfectly until a date and then fail completely, for every user of that domain at once. At 500 domains with 90-day ACME certificates you have roughly six renewals a day happening automatically, and the failure modes are all silent until they aren't: a DNS-01 challenge failing because a customer changed their nameservers, a rate limit hit during a bulk re-issue, a renewal job that has been erroring for three weeks into a log nobody reads. The secondary limit is memory and handshake CPU — 500 certificates and their chains held in memory per process, plus SNI-based certificate selection on every handshake — but that's the tractable problem.

It presents as a hard outage for one tenant with everything else healthy, which is the diagnostic shape: your aggregate error rate barely moves, your uptime SLO looks fine, and one customer is completely down. The controls are unglamorous and non-negotiable: alert on days-until-expiry for every certificate at 30, 14 and 7 days rather than on renewal-job success, because a job that silently stopped running produces no failures to alert on; monitor ACME challenge success rates as a leading indicator; and stagger renewals so a systemic failure doesn't align 500 expiries into one day. The reason to alert on the expiry date rather than the renewal process is that the date is the ground truth — it's true regardless of which part of your automation broke.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the TLS topology for a payments API: internet clients, a WAF requirement, and services that must mutually authenticate.

🎯 Really testing: whether you assign a termination model per hop from that hop's requirements, rather than picking one posture for the system.

The dominating constraint is that two requirements point in opposite directions: the WAF must read requests, which requires decryption at the edge, and the backend must authenticate callers cryptographically, which requires client certificates that only survive to their terminator. You cannot satisfy both with a single model, so the answer is necessarily per-hop — and saying that first is most of the answer.

The topology: internet client → edge terminates (TLS 1.3, the public certificate lives here, WAF and rate limiting run here on plaintext) → re-encrypts to the internal gateway with proxy_ssl_verify against your internal CA → gateway → mTLS between services, issued and rotated automatically by the mesh. Three hops, three postures, each justified by what that hop must do. The public certificate and the internal PKI are deliberately separate trust domains: a public CA vouches for you to browsers, and your internal CA vouches for services to each other, and mixing them means a public CA compromise reaches your service-to-service authentication.

The detail that carries this design is what happens to client identity at the edge. If a client presents a certificate for mTLS and the edge terminates, the backend sees a connection from the edge, not from the client — the identity has been consumed. The standard fix is for the terminator to validate the client certificate and forward its details in a header (X-Forwarded-Client-Cert in Envoy, or an equivalent), which means the backend's trust in that header is now entirely dependent on the edge stripping any client-supplied copy of it. That stripping rule is the single most important line of configuration in this design, and it's the one most often missed: an inbound X-Forwarded-Client-Cert that isn't cleared is an authentication bypass.

The failure I'd monitor first is certificate expiry across all three tiers, at 30/14/7 days, ahead of any latency or error metric. Every other failure here degrades; certificate expiry is binary and total, and it's the way this design most plausibly takes the payments API down. Second is the ratio of mTLS-authenticated to unauthenticated internal connections — if a service starts accepting plaintext or unverified connections because someone fixed a deploy problem by relaxing verification, nothing errors and the zero-trust property is quietly gone.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Terminate Pass-through (L4) Re-encrypt
Proxy decrypts? Yes, stops there Never Yes, then re-encrypts
Encrypted to backend? No — plaintext hop Yes, end-to-end Yes, new session
Routing granularity Path, header, method SNI (hostname) only Path, header, method
WAF / inspection ✅ ❌ ✅
Header rewriting ✅ ❌ ✅
Per-request balancing ✅ ❌ — connections only ✅
Request-level metrics ✅ status codes, latency ❌ bytes and connections ✅
Client cert reaches backend ❌ consumed at edge ✅ backend validates it ❌ forwarded in a header
Certificates needed Edge only Backend only Edge and backend
Crypto cost 1× ~0 at the proxy ~2×
Typical use Public web, CDN edge Regulated end-to-end, TCP multi-tenancy Regulated with L7 needs; the mesh default

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Open the envelope, forward it sealed, or open it and re-seal it.

📖 Story

A courier reaches the mailroom with a sealed envelope. The clerk can open it, read the address inside and hand the loose pages onward — fast, and the pages travel bare after that. Or pass it on still sealed, having read only what's written on the outside. Or open it, read it, and put the pages into a fresh envelope of the mailroom's own before sending it on — which takes two envelopes and twice the handling, and is the only way to both read it and keep it sealed.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • Opening and reading = terminating; the clerk can now sort by contents (path, headers, WAF rules)

  • Loose pages onward = the plaintext hop to the backend

  • Reading only the outside = SNI in the clear, which is all an L4 pass-through proxy gets

  • A fresh envelope of the mailroom's own = re-encryption on a new TLS session with the proxy's own certificate

  • Two envelopes, twice the handling = two handshakes and roughly double the crypto cost

  • The original sender's wax seal, destroyed on opening = the client certificate, consumed at the terminator and only reconstructible as a forwarded header

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism is entirely about where the encryption boundary sits relative to the decision boundary. A proxy can act on what it can read; TLS decides what it can read; so the termination model determines the proxy's entire capability set. Everything in Section 4's table follows from that one sentence.

Two details carry the discussion weight.

SNI is why pass-through isn't useless. The ClientHello's server_name extension (RFC 6066 §3) is plaintext, because the server must select a certificate before any keys exist. An L4 proxy can therefore peek at the first packet, extract the hostname, and route the connection — hostname-level routing with the TLS session intact end to end. This is ssl_preread in nginx's stream module and SNI-based routing in an NLB or a TLS-passthrough ingress. It's the reason "L4 means no routing at all" is wrong, and it's the middle ground people forget exists.

Client certificates do not survive termination. A client certificate authenticates the client to whoever terminates the TLS connection. If the edge terminates, the backend's connection comes from the edge, and the client's identity has been consumed. Recovering it means the terminator validates the certificate and forwards its details in a header — Envoy's X-Forwarded-Client-Cert, or equivalents elsewhere. That works, and it moves the trust: the backend now trusts a header, which is only sound if the edge strips any inbound copy of that header first. An unstripped forwarded-client-cert header is an authentication bypass, and it's the most consequential single misconfiguration in this whole topic.

Crypto cost arithmetic per request. Terminate: 1 handshake (client side) + 1 symmetric stream. Baseline 1×. Pass-through: 0 handshakes at the proxy — it copies bytes. ~0× at the proxy, pushed to the backend. Re-encrypt: 2 handshakes + 2 symmetric streams. ~2×.

The asymmetry that makes re-encryption affordable in practice: the client-side handshake is per-connection and unavoidable, while the backend connection is pooled and long-lived, so its handshake amortises across thousands of requests. Real-world re-encryption overhead is therefore much closer to 1.1× than 2× on request-heavy traffic — the 2× figure is the per-connection worst case, and quoting it without the amortisation caveat overstates the cost.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is what your proxy dashboard can show you. Terminate and you get status codes, per-path latency, per-request error rates and WAF decisions; pass through and you get connections, bytes and TCP resets. That difference decides whether a 3am incident is a five-minute triage or an hour of guessing, and it's the cost people consistently underweight when choosing pass-through for its security properties.

The second observable is certificate count and expiry surface. Termination concentrates certificates at the edge, where one team owns them and automation is mature. Re-encryption spreads them to every backend, and pass-through pushes them entirely to backends that may have no certificate automation at all. Each model implies a different lifecycle problem, and certificate expiry is the failure mode in this topic most likely to cause a total outage — it doesn't degrade, it stops.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# 1. TERMINATE — decrypt here, plaintext to the backend.
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/public.crt;    # the public CA cert lives here
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/public.key;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://backend;               # note: http, not https
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;  # backend can't tell otherwise
    }
}

# 2. RE-ENCRYPT — decrypt, act, then open a NEW TLS session upstream.
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/public.crt;
    location / {
        proxy_pass https://backend;              # https: second TLS session
        proxy_ssl_verify       on;               # ← without this you have
        proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/ssl/internal-ca.crt;  #   encryption
        proxy_ssl_name         backend.internal; #   but NOT authentication
        proxy_ssl_certificate  /etc/ssl/edge-client.crt;  # our cert, for mTLS
        proxy_ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/edge-client.key;
    }
}

# 3. PASS-THROUGH — never decrypt; route on SNI from the ClientHello.
stream {
    map $ssl_preread_server_name $upstream_pool {
        api.example.com   api_backends;
        app.example.com   app_backends;
        default           api_backends;
    }
    server {
        listen 443;
        ssl_preread on;          # peek at the ClientHello without terminating
        proxy_pass $upstream_pool;
    }
}

# 4. The critical strip rule when forwarding client identity (see Section 6).
# Clear any client-supplied copy BEFORE setting your own, or it's a bypass.
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Client-Cert $ssl_client_escaped_cert;

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

A request to api.example.com/v1/payments through the Section 8 re-encryption config, edge in ap-south-1, backend in the same VPC:

📥 t=0ms      Client opens connection to the edge
    │
    ▼
🔒 [1] TCP + TLS 1.3 handshake, client ↔ edge          t=0-42ms   (2 RTT @ 21ms)
    │      edge presents the PUBLIC cert for api.example.com
    │      SNI in ClientHello was plaintext — the edge used it to pick the cert
    ▼
🔓 [2] Edge decrypts the request                        t=42ms
    │      now readable: GET /v1/payments, headers, body
    │      WAF inspects, rate limiter checks, path routing decides
    ▼
🛡️ [3] Edge STRIPS inbound X-Forwarded-Client-Cert      t=42ms
    │      then sets it from the validated client cert
    ▼
🔐 [4] Edge → backend on a POOLED TLS session           t=42ms   (+0 RTT)
    │      session established at pool-warm time, NOT now
    │      proxy_ssl_verify on → backend cert checked against internal CA
    ▼
⚙️ [5] Backend decrypts, processes                       t=43-61ms
    │
    ▼
🔐 [6] Response encrypted on session 2, decrypted at
    │      the edge, re-encrypted on session 1           t=61ms
    ▼
🎯 [7] Client receives response                          t=82ms
       Two TLS sessions. Zero plaintext on any wire.

[1] Two round trips, and the SNI in the ClientHello was readable by anything on the path — the edge needed it to select a certificate, which is exactly why an L4 device could have routed on it too.

[2] This is the moment the whole note is about. The request is plaintext inside the edge process, which is what makes the WAF, the rate limiter and path-based routing possible. Under pass-through, none of steps 2 or 3 could happen.

[3] The strip-then-set order is the security-critical line. Reversed or omitted, a client can assert any identity it likes and the backend will believe it.

[4] The second TLS session costs zero additional round trips here because the edge-to-backend connection is pooled and was established earlier. This is why re-encryption's real overhead is far below the 2× per-connection figure — the expensive half is amortised. proxy_ssl_verify on is what makes this authentication rather than merely encryption.

[5–7] Total 82ms, of which 42ms is the client-side handshake and ~18ms is actual backend work. Under termination-only, step 4 would be plaintext and the total would be roughly 78ms — a ~5% latency cost for encryption-everywhere, which is the number to bring when someone claims re-encryption is expensive.

10. When TO Use This

  • Terminate at the edge when you need L7 capability and your internal network is a trust boundary you accept. Public websites, CDNs, anything where a WAF and path routing are the point and the backend hop is inside a VPC you control. It's the simplest model and the right default for most public traffic.

  • Pass through when the backend must see the client's certificate, or when a compliance requirement genuinely says no intermediary may decrypt. Also when you're fronting arbitrary TCP protocols and SNI-level routing is all you need — multi-tenant ingress, database proxies.

  • Re-encrypt when you need both L7 visibility and no plaintext anywhere. Regulated environments, payments, healthcare, and any service mesh — this is what a mesh does between sidecars, and the reason it's the mesh default is that it's the only model satisfying both requirements at once.

  • Mix them per hop. The edge and the internal gateway have different requirements; a single posture across the whole system will be wrong for at least one hop. Choosing per hop is the architect-level move here.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't pass through when you'll need to debug HTTP. The degradation is not in performance but in observability: your metrics become connections and bytes, and an incident that would have been "look at the 502 rate by path" becomes packet-level guesswork. Teams choose pass-through for its security story and discover this cost during their first bad outage.

  • Don't re-encrypt without proxy_ssl_verify or its equivalent. Encrypting to a backend whose certificate you never validate gives you the compliance checkbox and no authentication — anything that can win the route to that address can impersonate your backend. It's extremely common, because encryption-without-verification works fine in testing.

  • Don't forward client identity in a header without stripping the inbound copy. An unstripped X-Forwarded-Client-Cert (or X-Forwarded-For, or any identity header) lets a client assert whatever it likes. This is an authentication bypass, not a hardening nicety.

  • Don't terminate at the edge if the backend needs to make authorization decisions on client certificates. The identity is consumed at the terminator. Either pass through, or accept that the backend is trusting the edge's assertion — and be explicit about which, because the two have very different blast radii if the edge is compromised.

  • Don't assume re-encryption doubles your latency. The backend leg is pooled, so its handshake amortises; the measured cost on request-heavy traffic is a few percent. Quoting 2× as a latency figure rather than a per-connection crypto figure argues against a control you probably want.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "TLS pass-through means the load balancer can't do anything."

✅ Reality: SNI is plaintext in the ClientHello, so an L4 proxy can route by hostname without terminating — ssl_preread in nginx, SNI routing in an NLB. It's genuinely useful middle ground: hostname-level routing with end-to-end encryption intact. What you lose is everything below the hostname: paths, headers, methods, status codes.

❌ Misconception: "Re-encryption means the connection is end-to-end encrypted."

✅ Reality: It's two separate encrypted connections with a plaintext moment inside the proxy's memory. That's a meaningfully different security property from pass-through, where no intermediary can read anything. Both are "encrypted in transit"; only one is end-to-end, and conflating them in a compliance conversation is a real mistake.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I thought terminating at the edge and re-encrypting to the backend gave the backend the client's identity, since the client had presented a certificate. It doesn't — the certificate authenticated the client to the edge, and the backend's connection originates from the edge. Everything after that is the edge asserting the client's identity in a header, which the backend believes only because it trusts the edge. Once I saw that, the strip-the-inbound-header rule stopped looking like hygiene and started looking like the load-bearing control it is.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Presenting it as a binary. Terminate or pass-through, with re-encryption forgotten. Re-encryption is the answer to the most common real requirement — L7 capability plus no plaintext — and it's what every service mesh does. Naming three models rather than two is the first signal.

Saying "it's encrypted end-to-end" about re-encryption. It isn't, and someone in a compliance conversation will know. Say "encrypted on every hop, with a decryption point at the proxy" — which is accurate and still satisfies most requirements.

Forgetting SNI. "L4 can't route" is wrong and easy to correct. Knowing that the hostname is readable without decryption, and why it must be, is a reliable depth marker on this topic.

Not accounting for client certificates. If the discussion involves mTLS and you place a terminating proxy in the path without mentioning that the identity stops there, you've designed something that doesn't work. This is the most common structural error in mesh-adjacent designs.

Quoting the 2× crypto cost as a latency cost. They're different: the crypto doubles per connection, the latency impact on pooled request traffic is a few percent. The imprecise version argues against a control you probably want, which is a bad outcome from a technically true statement.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Crypto cost, re-encryption ~2× per connection Two handshakes, two symmetric streams Derived from RFC 8446 §2
Latency cost, re-encryption A few percent on pooled traffic Backend handshake amortises across the pooled connection Section 9 trace
SNI visibility Plaintext in ClientHello, always Required — server picks a cert before keys exist RFC 6066 §3
Certificate visibility Encrypted in TLS 1.3, plaintext in 1.2 Affects what a passive observer learns at each model RFC 8446 §2
Client cert scope Valid only to the terminator Beyond it, identity is a forwarded header RFC 8446 §4.4.2
Certificates to manage Terminate: edge only · Pass-through: backends only · Re-encrypt: both The lifecycle burden each model implies —
Handshake cost driver Asymmetric crypto, per connection Why TLS capacity is handshakes/sec, not Gbps RFC 8446 §2

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Pass-through adds nothing at the proxy; re-encryption adds a handshake that pooling amortises to a few percent
💰 Cost Re-encryption roughly doubles crypto CPU per connection and doubles the certificate inventory you must automate
🔒 Security / visibility The core trade of the topic: pass-through maximises confidentiality and minimises visibility; termination does the reverse. Re-encryption buys both at the price of a decryption point
📈 Scale Termination concentrates certificate lifecycle at one tier that can automate it; pass-through pushes it to backends that often can't
🔧 Ops complexity Each encryption boundary is a certificate, a rotation schedule and an expiry alert. Re-encryption means internal PKI stops being optional
🐛 Debuggability Pass-through is the single largest observability sacrifice available in this folder — connections and bytes instead of requests and status codes

16. Real World Usage

Service meshes are re-encryption as a product. Istio, Linkerd and Consul terminate at the sidecar, apply policy and telemetry on plaintext inside the pod, then re-encrypt with mTLS to the next sidecar. The automatic certificate issuance and rotation is the genuinely hard part they solve — it's what makes per-hop re-encryption operationally survivable at hundreds of services, and the reason building it by hand is rarely a good trade.

Cloud load balancers expose the models as product choices, which is worth knowing because it turns this decision into an infrastructure constraint. An AWS ALB terminates and can re-encrypt to an HTTPS target group; an NLB with a TLS listener terminates at L4, and with a TCP listener passes through so the target terminates. Choosing pass-through therefore also means choosing a different load-balancer product with different capabilities — the TLS decision and the LB decision aren't separable.

Certificate expiry remains the dominant outage mode in this area, and the well-documented cases are instructive because none were performance problems. Microsoft Teams went down in February 2020 on an expired certificate; an Ericsson certificate expiry in December 2018 took down mobile data for O2 and SoftBank customers; the Let's Encrypt DST Root CA X3 expiry in September 2021 broke HTTPS for older Android and OpenSSL 1.0.2 clients across a large swathe of the internet. Every termination point you add is another date on that list.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • SNI — Server Name Indication. The plaintext hostname in the ClientHello, sent because the server must choose a certificate before any keys exist. It's what makes hostname routing possible without decryption, and the last significant destination leak in TLS 1.3.

  • mTLS — mutual TLS. Both sides present certificates. Relevant here because the client's certificate authenticates it only to the terminator, which is what constrains where you may terminate.

  • XFCC — X-Forwarded-Client-Cert, Envoy's header for forwarding validated client-certificate details past a termination point. Useful, and only as trustworthy as the edge's rule about stripping inbound copies.

  • WAF — Web Application Firewall. Inspects request contents, so it requires decryption — the single most common reason a hop must terminate.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)
